queries: In our investigation of the neurotrophic potential of citrus by-products, we examined the effects of peel and pulp extracts from a defined panel of citrus cultivars on brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) secretion in ACHN renal adenocarcinoma cell cultures. The experimental design involved treating ACHN cells with standardized aqueous and ethanolic extracts prepared from both the flavedo/mesocarp (peel) and the juice sacs (pulp) of each selected cultivar. After a 24-hour incubation period, conditioned media were collected and BDNF concentrations were quantified using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Our results demonstrated that extracts from certain cultivars significantly upregulated BDNF levels in the culture medium, while others showed negligible or inhibitory effects. The differential response was attributed to variations in flavonoid and polymethoxyflavone profiles among the cultivars. Notably, the peel extracts generally exhibited a more pronounced effect on BDNF secretion compared to pulp extracts, likely due to higher concentrations of bioactive compounds in the outer tissues. The study included a total of ten distinct citrus cultivars, encompassing sweet oranges, mandarins, lemons, limes, and grapefruit. For each cultivar, both peel and pulp were independently processed and tested in triplicate, yielding twenty separate extract conditions. Statistical analysis using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post-hoc test revealed significant differences between treatment groups. These findings suggest that citrus peel and pulp extracts hold promise as natural modulators of BDNF expression, with potential implications for neurodegenerative disease prevention. Further fractionation studies are warranted to identify the specific phytochemicals responsible for the observed bioactivity.

Summary.
Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a neurotrophin that plays fundamental roles in neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. Its upregulation in the brain can effectively prevent and treat central nervous system (CNS) diseases, including depression, Alzheimer’s disease (AD), and Parkinson’s disease (PD). BDNF is synthesized in various peripheral tissues as well as in the brain and can be transported from peripheral circulation into the brain through the blood–brain barrier. Therefore, foods that upregulate BDNF in peripheral tissues may be beneficial in preventing and treating these CNS diseases. Previously, we revealed that treatment with Chinpi (Citrus unshiu peel) and Citrus natsudaidai increased BDNF levels in the human renal adenocarcinoma cell line ACHN. Here, we evaluated the effects of 21 citrus cultivars on BDNF production in ACHN cells by measuring BDNF levels in the cell culture medium. We found that treatment with peels and pulps of 13 citrus varieties increased BDNF levels in ACHN cells. ods are not delivered to the brain directly. Therefore, peripheral BDNF-upregulating foods are considered to elicit prophylactic and treatment effects in CNS diseases, such as depression, AD, and PD. Previously, we revealed that the human renal adenocarcinoma cell line ACHN produces and secretes BDNF and is useful in screening for molecular players leading to BDNF upregulation (24). We have shown that treatment with foxtail millet, Citrus unshiu peel (crude drug; Chinpi), and Citrus natsudaidai peel and pulp significantly increased BDNF levels in the culture medium of ACHN cells (24–26). In particular, the increased levels of BDNF by the citrus species were potent, suggesting that citrus plants and cultivars can upregulate BDNF production in ACHN cells.

Effects of citrus flavonoids on BDNF levels in ACHN cells.
Citrus cultivars contain numerous flavonoids, such as hesperetin, hesperidin, naringenin, naringin, neo-hesperidin, and nobiletin. Therefore, we investigated whether some flavonoids rich in citrus are involved in citrus-induced BDNF increase in ACHN cells. Consequently, 50 μmol/L nobiletin increased BDNF concentrations in the culture medium by approximately 1.2-fold, whereas other flavonoids did not exhibit BDNF-upregulating effects at 50 and 100 μmol/L (Fig. 4). None of the citrus flavonoids significantly increased the viability of ACHN cells (Table 4).





BDNF Upregulation by Citrus Cultivars

Effects of citrus cultivar peel and pulp on BDNF mRNA levels in ACHN cells.
We examined the transcript levels of BDNF mRNA in ACHN cells treated with peels and pulps of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott. These four citrus cultivars are consumed as edible fruits in many countries, and those BDNF-upregulating effects were potent. BDNF mRNA expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott peel was 1.68-, 1.48-, 1.44-, and 1.69-fold higher, respectively, than that in the control (Fig. 3).

In the pulp treatment group, BDNF expression in ACHN cells treated with 100 g/mL of Okitsuwase, Ponkan, Clementine mandarin, and Murcott pulp was 2.23-, 1.33-, 1.40-, and 1.67-fold higher, respectively, than that in control (Fig. 3).

In this study, we demonstrated that treatment with certain citrus peels and pulps elevated BDNF mRNA levels in ACHN cells. BDNF transcription is regulated by the CREB signaling pathway (41, 42), and CREB is activated by phosphorylation at Ser-133 (43). CREB phosphorylation is regulated by various signaling pathways, including phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B (Akt), cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA), Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CaMK), and Ras/Raf/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathways (42, 44, 45). We previously reported that treatment with the peel of C. unshiu (Chinpi) increased BDNF levels in ACHN cells, and this effect was attenuated by Akt, PKA, and MEK inhibitors but not by CaMK inhibitors (25). It is possible that citrus cultivars used in this study also upregulate BDNF levels via the Akt, PKA, and MEK pathways.
